title: Harmonizing as a kid, the mandolin, and the first banjo
summary: He harmonizes with boyhood friends in Defiance, learns scales on Butch Henline's mandolin, chords from Philip Sherman, then gets a banjo and plays square dances.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: And, I immediately wanted to pick it up and play it. Of course, which I couldn't do, but I first found out that I had anything musical involved - there was a bunch of kids, we used to go down along the river where I was born and, uh, ---

Yeah - Defiance, Ohio and, uh, we would harmonize and this is when we were kids of about seven years old - eight years old and it was amazing to find that you could find the harmony - like "Auld Lang Syne" and barber shop chords and barber shop harmony to songs that we used to play or sing and that's when I got the idea that it was easy for me to find what would be, in a growing up quartet, would be the baritone part. And, we had a kid that could also sing wonderful tenor and it was amazing what we put together as kids - you know - without any instruction at all and that's when I realized that music was for me. I just had to play an instrument too along with all that. And, so, my father used to have a cottage down along the Auglaize River on the way to Toledo -- it was called the "Independence Dam" and he had a cottage where he used to go fishing. And, he had a friend who was called Butch Henline, who was-- had later in his years became a second-string catcher for the Chicago White Sox and I used to go down there on Saturday-- of course, there was no school for me and I'd take my bike and ride down there. It was about six or seven miles and, uh, his friend used to

play the mandolin and he used to play mandolin and sing little songs along with it and that fascinated me. So, it took quite a bit of doing on my part because he didn't want to be bothered with any kids, I'm sure at that time. But, I'd ask him if he could just please show me how to make a scale. So, he actually taught me how to run the scale on this thing and, from there, I got to play all the old time songs. I could pick them out by myself after I learned to do the scale - the half-tone scale and regular scale and then I had a friend called Philip Sherman who lived across the river from me and he had a mandola, which is just a little bit bigger than a mandolin and he could cord on that thing. And, that was fascinating to me too. So, he taught me all the chords. So, then, when you get that far, then the next thing is, of course, in those days, was to have a banjo, which I got a banjo from a friend who had one. It was a pretty rickety one -- needed a new head and all that but I got it, and with the help of Phil Sherman, he got me playing in three or four keys of the chords. So, I got enough chords together in that Summer that Fall, I was asked to play in a group that played square dances. Of course, that's hill billy style music as you know and I got to like the chord to those things; gee, that was absolutely wonderful, I thought. And, uh, of course, my folks didn't-- first of all, they didn't want me to play and they didn't think I should stay out late at night - so, I used to pretend I went to bed and crawled out the window and

on Saturday nights, I'd play this hoedown music and then they started throwing in what they call "round music", that was fox trot and I got to learn the chords and play some of those songs. And, of course, they didn't have much choice about me because I was the only banjo player in town - so, they either had to have me or no banjo. So, I was pretty awful at first.
